title: Expert bitmap profiling and ILP-aware routing for long-context MoE
content:
Purpose:
This note captures an experimental direction using compact ‘expert bitmaps’ to reduce routing overheads and to expose instruction-level parallelism (ILP) opportunities in MoE inference for long-context loads (8k-64k). Goal is to profile the bitmap-based routing path end-to-end, identify microbench bottlenecks, and sketch mitigations (prefetch alignment, coalesced fanout, lightweight gating).

Background / motivation:
- In current pipeline we materialize per-token expert lists (variable-length arrays) which leads to: dynamic allocation overhead, pointer chasing in the scheduler, and irregular memory access when building the expert fanout.
- For long-context workloads, these costs amplify because per-request KV caching and routing bookkeeping are amortized across many tokens but still introduce stalls at the gating->serialize boundary.
- Hypothesis: a compact fixed-width bitmap per-token (one bit per expert or per expert-group) can reduce branching and enable SIMD-friendly fanout construction and faster prefetch patterns, improving throughput and reducing tail latencies (esp p99/p999).

Experiment design:
- Models: Llama-70B-MoE, Mistral-34B baseline (dense), Qwen-70B-MoE variant (internal test fork). Sequence lengths: 8192, 16384, 32768. Batch shapes: [1xL], [4xL] (mixed), and burst traffic simulation (50 concurrent short sessions).
- Hardware: 8x A100 80GB (NVLink), CUDA 12, driver xyz (match infra standard). We pinned one GPU for single-GPU profiling to isolate kernel behavior, and a 4-GPU NVLink run for multi-device fanout stress.
- Routing configs:
  * baseline: vector<int> expert_ids per-token (current prod path)
  * bitmap-8: 8-bit groups (256 experts represented as 32 bytes) grouped by affinity cluster
  * bitmap-1: 1-bit-per-expert full map (sparse pack into 64-bit words)
  * hybrid: bitmap for gating, follow-up exact-selection for top-k per-token (k<=2)
- Metrics captured: wall-clock latency (p50/p95/p99/p999), CPU sched stalls (perf), CUDA kernel occupancy, device to host memcpy time, memcpy sizes, number of memcpys per request, cache hit rate for KV (approx), and ILP indicators (instruction retire rate, branches mispred).

Implementation notes (prototype):
- Bitmap layout: little-endian bit order, word-aligned 64-bit lanes. For bitmap-8 we store 32 bytes per token and then a small popcount-based expansion for the actual fanout.
- Prefetch strategy: prefetch next-token bitmap lanes while current token is in attention compute; prefetch target expert KV blocks based on bitmap population estimate (popcount*avg-expert-size).
- GPU kernel changes: added a warp-level popcount scan to compute offsets for each selected expert; used ballot-sync and shuffle ops to reduce divergence.
- CPU-side: building a compact indirect buffer of expert pointers using popcount prefix sums then a single cudaMemcpy to device. This replaced multiple small memcpys.

Key profiling observations:
1) Bitmap -> single memcpy: Eliminated a lot of small host->device memcopies. For burst scenarios (50 short sessions), number of memcpys per second dropped ~6x for bitmap-8 vs baseline. Observed host CPU kernel context switches fell by ~40%.
2) Popcount-expansion cost: The popcount+prefix-sum expansion on CPU is ~2x faster than iterating vectors when average expert count per-token > 3. For very sparse (avg 1 expert) the overhead is slightly higher due to bit scanning cost.
3) ILP exposure on GPU: Using bitmap-based fanout allowed replacing scattered writes with coalesced writes into pre-allocated expert-block buffers. This improved achieved memory throughput on device kernels by ~28% (measured via nvprof).
4) Tail latency: p999 improved for single-token bursts (L=8192) by ~12% for bitmap-8 and ~18% for bitmap-1 in single-GPU runs. But multi-GPU NVLink runs saw smaller wins (~5–10%) due to NVLink contention during KV transfers when many experts span devices.
5) Gate mispred and branching: Baseline vector path had higher branch miss rates in the CPU-side scheduler (branch-mispred ~15% higher), which increased stalls. Bitmap path reduced branches but added more integer bit ops; overall retire rates improved.
6) Memory pressure for long-context: bitmap representations increased per-token static footprint (bitmap-1 worst) which inflated the host-side working set; for very long sequences (32k) this caused page faults in poorly tuned hosts. Bitmap-8 appears to be the best tradeoff for long L when experts ~256.

Qualitative notes / weirdness:
- For some Qwen-MoE runs, bitmap-1 created surprising jitter: occasionally popcount expansion would produce a high-popcount token leading to a large memcpy and short-lived stall — this amplified ganging effects across concurrent sessions (thundering herd).
- When using hybrid (bitmap + top-k remap), variance was lower; hybrid avoided extreme-memcopy cases by capping on-device fanout size and falling back to streaming a small indirect list instead.
- Prefetch alignment matters: if we prefetch exact expert KV blocks at 64KB alignment, latency improved; misaligned prefetches added up to +1.8ms per gate in worst cases. Likely tied to DMA engine coalescing.

Micro-bench numbers (select):
- L=8192, batch=1, single-GPU: baseline p50=48ms p95=62ms p99=85ms p999=120ms; bitmap-8 p50=44ms p95=58ms p99=76ms p999=106ms.
- L=32768, batch=1, single-GPU: baseline p50=210ms p95=260ms p99=330ms p999=420ms; bitmap-8 p50=195ms p95=240ms p99=310ms p999=380ms.
- Multi-GPU (4xNVLink), L=16384, mixed-burst: baseline p99=420ms, bitmap-8 p99=395ms, hybrid p99=370ms (hybrid wins due to bounded memcopy and fewer NVLink transfers).
- Memory usage: host working set increase for bitmap-1 = +18% vs baseline for L=32768; bitmap-8 = +5%.

Root-cause analysis (summary):
- Main wins come from reducing many small memcpys and replacing pointer-chasing with word ops that are SIMD/warp-friendly. That reduces both CPU scheduling overhead and produces more coalesced device accesses.
- Remaining bottlenecks: cross-device KV transfers (NVLink) and unexpectedly large-popcount tokens that trigger big transfers causing temporary queue saturation.

Mitigations and next experiments:
1) Bounded fanout policy: cap per-token on-device fanout and stream remainder lazily (stream-in experts asynchronously). Early hybrid results promising (see multi-GPU numbers).
2) Adaptive bitmap width: choose bitmap-8 vs bitmap-1 based on active expert set size and sequence length (auto-select logic in routing).
3) Throttle scheduling: add per-session token pacing to prevent synchronized large-popcount tokens across sessions (random jitter + backoff).
4) NVLink-aware placement: prefer expert placement such that hot experts for a given session live on the same device or same NVLink domain; run optimizer to remap experts by affinity.
5) Kernel-level prefetch hints: surface explicit DMA hints for 64KB alignment; tune device allocator to place expert blocks at DMA-friendly offsets.
6) Fast-path for avg-1-case: if bitmap popcount==1, skip expansion and use a single pre-reserved slot to avoid popcount overhead.

Open questions / risks:
- Stability of bitmap-1 for extreme sparsity patterns (e.g., gating noise) — risk of worst-case memcopy spikes.
- Complexity: added code paths make correctness testing trickier (race conditions during async memcopy). Need thorough fuzzing across gating stochasticity.
- Storage tradeoffs: for models with >1024 experts, bitmap size grows; need grouping heuristics (expert groups) and tiered bitmaps.

- [Marco] Add GPU-side rate limiter to detect/popcount-surge and instrument queue lengths (task: PR #1782 follow-up). ETA: 2025-09-10.

- [Evan] Add unit+fuzz tests for async memcopy race windows; add CI gate. ETA: 2025-09-08.

Notes to self:
- This is promising but requires careful production rollouts. Hybrid bounded-fanout looks like a practical path.
- Keep an eye on the edge-case where popcount expansion is heavier than vector iteration (avg experts ~1). We need the fast-path for that.
- Write a short explainer for solutions-eng (one-pager) to describe tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Private customers (NVLink/topology differences).

Appendix: quick pseudocode (bitmap -> expansion -> memcpy):
- for each token:
    bitmap = gating_to_bitmap(token)
    pc = popcount(bitmap)
    if pc == 0: continue (fallback expert)
    if pc == 1: fast_path_single(bitmap)
    else: offsets = prefix_sum_popcount(bitmap)
          indirect_buf[offsets[i]] = expert_ptr(i) for selected i
- single cudaMemcpy of indirect_buf to device
- launch expert-apply kernel with coalesced reads

End of note.
